title: The Stream Above the Yellowstone to the Cheyenne River: Low Dog, the Charge on the Second Column, and the Account Given to the Newspaper
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Powder River country, a son born to the Oglala
stops.date_confidence: year only, and contested: Wikipedia gives c. 1846, indigenouspeople.net gives ca. 1847; no source names a month, a day, or a camp, and the location is a reconstruction from Oglala range in the period
stops.campa: A son is born to the Oglala somewhere in the hunting country between the Powder and the Tongue, and nothing that survives names the camp, the bend of the river, or the day. He is called Sunka Khuciyela, Low Dog. The buffalo herds are still whole. The Bozeman road is not yet cut through this country and the treaty that will call these grounds unceded is more than twenty years off. Everything the record will ever hold about the beginning of his life will come later, out of his own mouth, into a newspaper printed a thousand miles east of here.
suggested_refs: The unceded Powder River hunting grounds, Oglala range in the 1840s

stops.name: The mouth of the Yellowstone, the first war path
stops.date_confidence: year inferred from his stated age of fourteen at the 1881 interview; the pool's first pass placed this fight on the Milk River, roughly 300 km off, and that coordinate is corrected here to the Missouri-Yellowstone confluence
stops.campa: At fourteen he leaves camp against his parents and rides north with a war party to a stream above the place where the Yellowstone empties into the Missouri. An Assiniboine band is hunting buffalo there. In the account he gives a newspaper twenty-one years later he kills one of their men. The sources that credit him with the chief's title for this fight say he killed two of them in it, and nothing in the record reconciles the counts. He tells this story first, before the Custer fight and before anything else, to a room of army officers at an agency, as the thing about himself worth saying at the start.
stops.quote: I went against the will of my parents and those having authority over me. It was on a stream above the mouth of the Yellowstone. We went to war against a band of Assiniboins that were hunting buffalo, and I killed one of their men.
stops.quote_source: Low Dog, interview account, Leavenworth Weekly Times, 18 August 1881, reprinted in W. A. Graham, The Custer Myth (Stackpole, 1953), pp. 74-76
suggested_refs: The Missouri-Yellowstone confluence, later the site of Fort Buford
sources: Low Dog's account, Leavenworth Weekly Times, 18 August 1881, in Graham, The Custer Myth

stops.name: Oglala camp, a war chief at fourteen
stops.date_confidence: year inferred from his stated age; month arbitrary, no source dates the recognition
stops.campa: They make him a war chief on the strength of that fight, and he is fourteen years old. No account describes the ceremony or names the men who agreed to it, and the two sources that carry the promotion name no document behind it. What the sources keep instead is the arithmetic: two enemies in one engagement, at fourteen. He holds the title through the Bozeman war and through the treaty that shuts the Powder River country to the whites, and he is thirty years old in the summer the great camp gathers on the Rosebud.
suggested_refs: The Lakota war-honor system of counted coups, by which a boy of fourteen could be raised to chief

segments.name: The Summer of the Great Camp

stops.name: Deer Medicine Rocks, the hundred cuts on the Rosebud
stops.date_confidence: early June attested; the coordinate is the canonical atlas pin inherited from sitting_bull.journey.json, and Wikipedia's own Deer Medicine Rocks entry gives 45.6950, -106.6917 instead, a discrepancy left standing rather than fixed in one file
stops.campa: At the sandstone bluff on Rosebud Creek where the old carvings are, Sitting Bull gives a hundred pieces of flesh cut from his arms and dances until he goes down. He sees soldiers falling into camp upside down, and the camp reads the vision as soldiers who will be killed. The circles gathered here are Hunkpapa, Oglala, Minneconjou, Sans Arc, Blackfeet Lakota, Cheyenne. No account names Low Dog at the rocks. He is an Oglala chief and the Oglala are here, and twenty days later the whole camp is over the divide.
suggested_refs: The petroglyph bluff at Deer Medicine Rocks, Rosebud County, Montana
sources: sitting_bull.journey.json, stop 'Deer Medicine Rocks on the Rosebud, the hundred cuts'

stops.name: The Rosebud, the battle nobody records him at
stops.date_confidence: date of the battle attested; Low Dog's presence is a reconstruction, and no source places him on this field or anywhere else that day
stops.campa: Crook comes up the Rosebud with fifteen hundred men and Crazy Horse fights him to a standstill through six hours of broken ground, after which Crook turns south to his supply camp and takes no further part in the summer. The Oglala are in this fight in strength. No source in this atlas puts Low Dog on the ground; no source puts him anywhere else either. Eight days from now the second column will come down on the great camp with Crook and his fifteen hundred nowhere on that field.
suggested_refs: Rosebud Battlefield State Park, Big Horn County, Montana
sources: sitting_bull.journey.json, stop 'The Rosebud, a battle he may not have fought'

stops.name: The Little Bighorn, the camp of ten thousand
stops.date_confidence: attested; the canonical Little Bighorn pin, inherited byte-identical from sitting_bull.journey.json
stops.campa: The village stands along the west bank of the Greasy Grass, six circles strung out more than three miles, roughly eighteen hundred lodges by the count an army captain makes afterward. Hunkpapa at the upper end, Cheyenne at the lower, the Oglala among the circles between. Cottonwood belts hide the lodges from the bluffs across the water. Ten thousand people are camped here and the pony herds run out over the benchland to the west. Some horses go missing that day and a man rides back down the trail to look for them.
stops.quote: We were in camp near Little Big Horn river. We had lost some horses, and an Indian went back on the trail to look for them.
stops.quote_source: Low Dog, Leavenworth Weekly Times, 18 August 1881, in Graham, The Custer Myth, pp. 74-76
suggested_refs: Captain Weir's estimate of some 1,800 lodges in the combined village
sources: Low Dog's account, Leavenworth Weekly Times, 18 August 1881
sitting_bull.journey.json, stop 'The Little Bighorn, the camp of ten thousand'

stops.name: The Oglala circle, the alarm at noon
stops.date_confidence: attested; the hour comes from Low Dog's own gesture at the sun during the 1881 interview
stops.campa: The horse-hunters come in with word of soldiers on the back trail. Low Dog is asleep in his lodge with the sun straight overhead. He hears the crier and does not believe him, having heard false alarms before in a camp this size. Then the firing starts at the upper end, where Reno's line has dismounted and is shooting into the Hunkpapa lodges, and the women and children begin running north through the circles with what they can carry. He gets up and calls for his horse. He has been a war chief for twenty-one years, and the fighting that starts at this hour is over before evening.
stops.quote: I was asleep in my lodge at the time. The sun was about noon (pointing with his finger). I heard the alarm, but I did not believe it. I thought it was a false alarm.
stops.quote_source: Low Dog, Leavenworth Weekly Times, 18 August 1881, in Graham, The Custer Myth, pp. 74-76
suggested_refs: The 1881 newspaper transcript, which preserves the reporter's note of his gesture at the sun
sources: Low Dog's account, Leavenworth Weekly Times, 18 August 1881, in Graham, The Custer Myth

stops.name: The upper ford, Reno driven back across the river
stops.date_confidence: attested; his presence in the valley fight rests on his own testimony, dictated five years afterward
stops.campa: Reno's three companies come at the southern end of the village on foot, hold a skirmish line in front of the Hunkpapa circle, fall back into the timber, then break out of it altogether, across the river and up the bluffs on the far side with Lakota riding among them the whole way. Low Dog is in this fight and says so plainly afterward. The soldiers who reach the top dig in and stay dug in there. With the upper end of the village no longer under fire, the men who drove them across the water turn downstream.
stops.quote: I do not say that Reno was a coward. He fought well, but our men were fighting to save their women and children, and drive them back.
stops.quote_source: Low Dog, Leavenworth Weekly Times, 18 August 1881, in Graham, The Custer Myth, pp. 74-76
suggested_refs: The Reno-Benteen defense site on the bluffs east of the river, held through the night of 25 June
sources: Low Dog's account, Leavenworth Weekly Times, 18 August 1881

stops.name: Medicine Tail Coulee, the second column turned from the water
stops.date_confidence: attested by John Stands In Timber, not by Low Dog: the 1881 narrative contains no ford or crossing reference at all, and the pool's coordinate for this ford was north of Last Stand Hill, which reverses the battle geography and is corrected here
stops.campa: A second column comes down a dry coulee toward the water below the village, and the warriors who have just finished with Reno ride north through the camp to meet it. John Stands In Timber, telling it long afterward from the Cheyenne side, puts Low Dog here, moving back and forth between the two fights and leaving the Reno ground to go down toward Custer. The column does not get across the river. It turns away from the ford and climbs the high ground to the north, and the men who turned it back come up the slopes behind it.
suggested_refs: John Stands In Timber's Cheyenne account of the movement between the two fights
sources: John Stands In Timber, Cheyenne account, as cited in the research pool

stops.name: Battle Ridge, the charge and the sentence
stops.date_confidence: attested, and the tag corrected: the pool first marked this quotation unverified on Wikipedia's warning, but the line is verbatim in the 1881 primary source, and Wikipedia's warning attaches to its own weak citation
stops.campa: He masses his men for the charge against the second column. So that no man should fall back, every man whips another man's horse. They come on, in his own telling, like a thunderbolt. The soldiers are dismounted on the high ground above the river, shooting from behind their own animals, and the charge goes into them out of the coulees. The colon in the sentence is his; the period that later replaces it belongs to other people, who will put the line in other men's mouths for a hundred years.
stops.quote: This is a good day to die: follow me.
stops.quote_source: Low Dog, Leavenworth Weekly Times, 18 August 1881, in Graham, The Custer Myth, pp. 74-76
suggested_refs: The 1881 text of the rallying cry, with its colon, before a century of paraphrase
sources: Low Dog's account, Leavenworth Weekly Times, 18 August 1881, in Graham, The Custer Myth

stops.name: Last Stand Hill, the end of the column
stops.date_confidence: attested; the coordinate is the battlefield monument, distinct from the canonical village and battlefield pin used elsewhere in this journey
stops.campa: The last of the column dies at the end of the ridge above the river, and Low Dog says afterward that none of them made any attempt to get away. He does not know who killed Custer. He does not learn until after the fighting is over that the white chief was on the field at all. Asked five years later, at an agency, in front of officers of the same army, what he thinks of the men he destroyed, he praises them without qualification, and the officers listening write it down.
stops.quote: I never before nor since saw men so brave and fearless as those white warriors.
stops.quote_source: Low Dog, Leavenworth Weekly Times, 18 August 1881, in Graham, The Custer Myth, pp. 74-76
suggested_refs: The Seventh Cavalry monument and the white marble markers on Last Stand Hill
sources: Low Dog's account, Leavenworth Weekly Times, 18 August 1881, in Graham, The Custer Myth

stops.name: The village, three men laid out in the lodges
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool placed this death at Deep Ravine, which no source supports, and the account itself puts the bodies in the village
stops.campa: In the village three dead men are laid out in tepees in rich dress. One of them is his brother, born of the same mother and the same father, and the other two he does not know. Thirty-eight of the camp's men die in the fight itself, and more die afterward of wounds than he can count, more in proportion to the killed than in any fight he has seen, and the horses with them. The column is destroyed and the camp that destroyed it will not exist as a camp by August.
stops.quote: One was his own brother, born of the same mother and the same father, and he did not know who the other two were.
stops.quote_source: Low Dog's 1881 account as rendered in Graham, The Custer Myth, pp. 74-76
suggested_refs: The Lakota and Cheyenne dead of 25 June 1876, never fully enumerated
sources: Low Dog's account, Leavenworth Weekly Times, 18 August 1881, in Graham, The Custer Myth

segments.name: The Scattering and the Line to the North

stops.name: The Bighorn foothills, the great camp comes apart
stops.date_confidence: the dispersal is attested in general; Low Dog's own movements in these weeks are not separately documented anywhere
stops.campa: Within days the camp breaks into the bands that made it, and the bands move off in different directions, toward the mountains and back toward the Powder River country. Ten thousand people and their horses cannot be fed in one valley for long, and three army columns are converging on this one. Low Dog's movements in these weeks are not recorded. The largest gathering of Lakota and Cheyenne anyone alive has seen lasts a few weeks and is never assembled again.
suggested_refs: The post-battle dispersal of the Little Bighorn camp, July 1876

stops.name: The Powder River drainage, the winter the sources do not agree on
stops.date_confidence: wholly unresolved: one account keeps him among the Powder River holdouts, Hardorff has him surrendering in May 1877 and leaving for Canada later, and the Spotted Tail ledger has him enrolling that September with Lame Deer's village
stops.campa: Through the winter Miles and Crook work the scattered bands, burning lodges and stores in the snow and taking surrenders one village at a time. Where Low Dog is during these months is the largest hole in his record. One account keeps him out here among the holdouts. Another has him surrendering in May and crossing to Canada afterward. A third has him coming in that September with Lame Deer's people, hundreds of miles south. The three cannot all be true and no document has been produced that decides between them.
suggested_refs: The winter campaign of 1876-77 in the Powder and Tongue river country
sources: R. G. Hardorff, The Death of Crazy Horse, p. 86, as quoted by american-tribes.com

stops.name: Spotted Tail Agency, the name entered in the ledger
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the Spotted Tail agency ledger book, page 64
stops.campa: On the fourth of September he enrolls at the Spotted Tail Agency on Beaver Creek, beside the post the army calls Camp Sheridan, coming in with the surrendering village of Lame Deer. His name goes onto page sixty-four of the ledger. Crazy Horse surrendered at the neighboring agency that spring and the country north of here is emptying out. The agency is crowded with people who came in that season and are being counted, issued rations, and told where they will be living next, which is not where they are standing.
suggested_refs: The Spotted Tail Agency enrollment ledger, page 64, entry of 4 September 1877
sources: american-tribes.com, 'Low Dog (Sunka Kucigala)', citing the Spotted Tail ledger book p. 64

stops.name: The sandhill country, the march ordered east to the Missouri
stops.date_confidence: autumn 1877 attested; the precise line of the route he walks is not fixed in any source
stops.campa: That autumn the government orders the Spotted Tail and Red Cloud people marched east to new agencies on the Missouri River, where steamboats can bring the supplies up and where the agencies will be easier to hold. The column moves out across the sandhills. Among the thousands on that road are people who came in only weeks ago, on the understanding that they would be allowed to stay in the country they came from. No source fixes the line of march that Low Dog walks, only that he is on it.
suggested_refs: The 1877 removal of the Nebraska agencies to the Missouri River

stops.name: Somewhere on the removal road, the column broken
stops.date_confidence: attested that he led the breakout; no source names the place or the day, and the month here is a placement within the autumn march
stops.campa: Somewhere on the march the column comes apart. Low Dog turns his people north instead of east, off the road to the Missouri and toward the British line, and others go with him. William Garnett, the interpreter, remembers thirty years later exactly who led them off and what he thought of him. The government counts the missing at the far end of the march. The agencies on the Missouri open that winter holding fewer people than were started east toward them, and the difference is walking north through the snow.
stops.quote: Low Dog, a northern chief an upstart who belonged to the Lame Deer band and was a brave man, he led these Indians off.
stops.quote_source: William Garnett, interview with Judge Eli Ricker, 1907, quoted on american-tribes.com
suggested_refs: The Eli Ricker interview transcripts, Nebraska State Historical Society
sources: american-tribes.com, 'Low Dog (Sunka Kucigala)', quoting the Ricker interviews

stops.name: Wood Mountain, over the forty-ninth parallel
stops.date_confidence: the crossing is a reconstruction from the general movement of the exile bands; the pool labelled this coordinate as the international boundary, and it is in fact Wood Mountain village, some 30 km north of the line
stops.campa: He crosses the line into the North-West Territories and comes up to the Wood Mountain country, where Sitting Bull has been camped since May with the Hunkpapa and with whoever else has made it north. The Mounted Police tell the refugees they may stay as long as they keep the peace, and that they will be given no rations, no reservation, and no protection if they raid back across the border. The buffalo on this side are thinning already. He stays north of the line for the next four years.
suggested_refs: The Lakota refugee camps in the Wood Mountain district, 1877-1881

stops.name: Fort Walsh, the post where the terms are set
stops.date_confidence: his presence is a reconstruction and no source names him here; the pool's coordinate was 5 km off and is corrected to Wikipedia's, and the post was NWMP headquarters 1878-1882
stops.campa: West of Wood Mountain, in the Cypress Hills, stands Fort Walsh, headquarters of the Mounted Police and the place through which the Canadian government conducts every piece of its business with the refugee Sioux. The exile bands move between the two districts with the hunting. No source puts Low Dog inside this stockade by name. The fort is where it is decided, in rooms he may or may not have entered, what the terms of his staying in this country are going to be, and for how long.
suggested_refs: Fort Walsh, NWMP headquarters in the Cypress Hills, 1878-1882

stops.name: The exile camp, a newspaperman writes down his face
stops.date_confidence: year attested from Finerty's visit; no month given
stops.campa: A Chicago newspaperman named John Finerty rides up to the camps to see the men who destroyed the Seventh Cavalry three years earlier, and he writes down what Low Dog looks like to him. Three words carry the whole surviving physical description of the man from anyone who stood in front of him: brave and sullen. No other contemporary account of his person is on record. What is known of how he looked comes from a reporter, and so does what is known of what he said.
stops.quote: brave and sullen. He had little to say, but was a man of considerable action when it came to blows.
stops.quote_source: John F. Finerty, describing Low Dog after an 1879 visit to Sitting Bull's camp in Canada, quoted on american-tribes.com
suggested_refs: John F. Finerty's despatches from the Sioux exile camps in Canada, 1879

segments.name: The Rifle Laid Down and the Account Given

stops.name: Fort Buford, the surrender at the confluence
stops.date_confidence: May 1881 comes from a note in the quotations pool; the geography pool gives his passage through Fort Buford only as 1880-1881 and states no exact date is recorded
stops.campa: He comes back across the line and gives himself up at the post standing where the Yellowstone runs into the Missouri, a day's ride from the stream where he took his first two enemies at fourteen. Sitting Bull will hand over his own rifle at this same fort on the nineteenth of July, through his son, and go down the river under guard. In the same years, at the other end of the hemisphere, Julio Argentino Roca is finishing the Conquista del Desierto against the nations of the pampas. He is about thirty-four years old.
suggested_refs: Fort Buford at the Missouri-Yellowstone confluence, where the northern surrenders were taken in 1881
sources: sitting_bull.journey.json, stop 'Fort Buford, the rifle handed over'

stops.name: Standing Rock Agency, onto the rolls at Fort Yates
stops.date_confidence: summer 1881 attested; no day recorded
stops.campa: The agency at Fort Yates takes him in that summer, in the same season the exile bands come back over the line in a body and are counted onto the rolls. The Hunkpapa who surrendered with Sitting Bull are held as prisoners of war and shipped down the Missouri to Fort Randall. Low Dog is not among them. He stays on the agency with his band and enters the part of his life that survives in ledgers rather than in fights: rations drawn, families listed, ages estimated, names written down by clerks who do not speak the language.
suggested_refs: The Standing Rock Agency at Fort Yates, Dakota Territory
sources: sitting_bull.journey.json, stop 'Fort Randall, twenty months a prisoner of war'

stops.name: Standing Rock, the officers ask about the Custer fight
stops.date_confidence: the interview precedes its publication on 18 August 1881; the account carries no place of interview and its location at the agency is an inference
stops.campa: A group of army officers sits down with him and puts questions about the Custer fight, with Captain Howe interpreting. He answers for the record: the alarm at noon, Reno driven back, the charge on the second column, thirty-eight dead. Then somebody asks what part Sitting Bull took in the fighting, and he gives the answer of a man who has no love for the Hunkpapa and does not intend to pretend otherwise in front of white officers. The newspaper prints it, and prints alongside it the plain observation that Low Dog is not friendly to Sitting Bull.
stops.quote: If some one would lend him a heart he would fight.
stops.quote_source: Low Dog, Leavenworth Weekly Times, 18 August 1881, in Graham, The Custer Myth, pp. 74-76
suggested_refs: The 1881 interview conducted through Captain Howe, interpreter
sources: Low Dog's account, Leavenworth Weekly Times, 18 August 1881, in Graham, The Custer Myth

stops.name: Leavenworth, the account set in type
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the pool's coordinate for Leavenworth was about 7 km west of the city and is corrected here
stops.campa: The account runs in the Weekly Times of Leavenworth, Kansas, on the eighteenth of August, eight hundred miles from the valley it describes. It is among the earliest Native accounts of the Little Bighorn to reach print, five years and two months after the day, and it will be reprinted by Graham, by Utley, by Hardorff, by Upton, by everyone since who wanted the fight told from inside the village. Sitting Bull, still a prisoner of war at Fort Randall, will give his own version to newspapermen after Low Dog and Gall have given theirs.
stops.quote: Now, I want to learn the white man's way, for I see that he is stronger than we are, and that his government is better than ours.
stops.quote_source: Low Dog, closing line of the interview, Leavenworth Weekly Times, 18 August 1881, in Graham, The Custer Myth, pp. 74-76
suggested_refs: The Leavenworth Weekly Times of 18 August 1881, reprinted in Graham, The Custer Myth, pp. 74-76
sources: Wikipedia, 'Low Dog', citing the Leavenworth Weekly Times
W. A. Graham, The Custer Myth (Stackpole, 1953)
sitting_bull.journey.json, stop 'Fort Randall, twenty months a prisoner of war'

stops.name: Standing Rock, the household written down
stops.date_confidence: December 1881 census attested; no day
stops.campa: The agency clerk writes him into the winter census: Sunka kucigala, Low Dog, age thirty-four; his wife Medicine, age thirty-five; two sons, One Who Makes Disorder and Horse. Twenty-two families of his band are listed under his name on the same rolls. The war chief made at fourteen for two enemies killed in one fight is now a household on a page in a government book. That page and the ones after it are the reason anything at all is known about the next thirty years of his life.
suggested_refs: The 1881 Standing Rock Agency census, listing Low Dog's band at twenty-two families
sources: american-tribes.com, 'Low Dog (Sunka Kucigala)', citing the 1881 Standing Rock Agency census

stops.name: Pine Ridge Agency, the Oglala sorted to their agency
stops.date_confidence: May 1882 attested; the pool's coordinate was the reservation centroid, some 55 km from the agency headquarters, and its description of Pine Ridge as newly established was wrong by four years
stops.campa: In May the Oglala at Standing Rock are moved to Pine Ridge on White Clay Creek, the agency Red Cloud's people have held since 1878, and Low Dog goes with them and his twenty-two families with him. Sorting the bands by tribe is the government's work in these years: Hunkpapa here, Oglala there, every name on a list belonging to one agency and drawing its rations from that one. The reservation itself does not exist in law yet. The act that carves the great Sioux reserve into six is seven years off.
suggested_refs: The Pine Ridge Agency on White Clay Creek, established 1878

segments.name: The Agency Years and the Minnesota Cell

stops.name: Standing Rock, Red Dog draws the deed in crayon
stops.date_confidence: year attested, no month; the source places the drawing at Standing Rock two years after the rolls transfer him to Pine Ridge, and that tension is left standing
stops.campa: A Lakota man named Red Dog takes crayons and agency paper and draws Low Dog's valor in battle, in the ledger manner: the horse, the man, the deed. The old counting of coups is being done now in the materials the agency issues, on the backs of accounts and in bound ledgers, because the painted robes and the winter counts are going out of use and paper is what the storehouse hands out. The drawing survives. Where its subject was living in 1884 is less certain than the drawing is.
suggested_refs: Red Dog's 1884 crayon ledger drawing commemorating Low Dog's valor

stops.name: Pine Ridge, the departure with no destination
stops.date_confidence: the source registers only that he had left by 1886; no departure date, no destination, and the following several years are blank
stops.campa: He leaves Pine Ridge before 1886, and the record notes only that he is gone. No destination and no reason are entered, only the year by which the absence has become visible on paper. Several years of his life fall into this hole and nothing has been found to fill them. Men leave agencies in these years for reasons the clerks do not write down, and no clerk wrote this one down. He appears on paper again four years later, at Cherry Creek, on another reservation entirely.
suggested_refs: The gap in the agency record between Pine Ridge before 1886 and Cherry Creek by 1890

stops.name: Cherry Creek, arrested over Big Foot's son
stops.date_confidence: year attested, no month; the sources give the charge in a single sentence and record no hearing and no outcome
stops.campa: He turns up at Cherry Creek on the Cheyenne River reservation, among Miniconjou and Sans Arc people, in the year the Ghost Dance comes up out of the south and the agents begin writing frightened letters to Washington. He is arrested there on the charge of trying to take Big Foot's young son by force, over the boy's refusal to go to the agency school. The sources give the charge and nothing else: no hearing, no outcome, no word from him about it, no statement of whether the boy was kin. Big Foot has under a year to live.
suggested_refs: Cherry Creek settlement, Cheyenne River Reservation, South Dakota

stops.name: Fort Snelling, a stone fort above the Mississippi
stops.date_confidence: the imprisonment is attested and lasted a few months across the winter of 1890-91; the month here places it before Wounded Knee, and the pool's claim that he was among Lakota removed east during the Ghost Dance unrest is an unsupported conflation with the Fort Sheridan prisoners and is dropped
stops.campa: He is taken east and locked up at Fort Snelling above the meeting of the Minnesota and the Mississippi, thirteen hundred miles from Cherry Creek, on a charge of attempted kidnapping. This is the winter the agencies fill with soldiers. On the fifteenth of December, at Standing Rock, Sitting Bull is killed by policemen of his own nation on the agency payroll, and the Hunkpapa scatter toward Big Foot's camp. Low Dog spends that month in a stone fort in Minnesota. The photographer Edward Bromley will make his picture here the following year.
suggested_refs: Edward Augustus Bromley's 1891 photograph of Low Dog, made during the Fort Snelling imprisonment
sources: sitting_bull.journey.json, stop 'Fort Yates, the coffin and the quicklime'

stops.name: Wounded Knee Creek, the ground he is not standing on
stops.date_confidence: the massacre is attested to the day; Low Dog is not present and no source places him here, and the canonical pin is inherited from sitting_bull.journey.json
stops.campa: Fourteen days after Sitting Bull is killed, the Seventh Cavalry surrounds Big Foot's people on this creek while they are being disarmed and kills some three hundred of them, more than half of them women and children. Big Foot dies in the snow. It is the same regiment Low Dog charged on the ridge above the Greasy Grass fourteen years earlier, and the boy he was arrested that year for trying to take was Big Foot's son. Low Dog is in a cell in Minnesota. No source records what he is told, or when, or by whom.
suggested_refs: The mass grave on the hill above Wounded Knee Creek
sources: sitting_bull.journey.json, stop 'Fort Yates, the coffin and the quicklime'

stops.name: Fort Bennett, handed back at the mouth of the Cheyenne
stops.date_confidence: August 1891 attested; no day
stops.campa: The local Indian agent writes a letter on his behalf and he is let out after a few months. In August he is escorted from Fort Snelling to Fort Bennett, the military post and agency headquarters at the mouth of the Cheyenne River, and handed back to his own people. He comes back to a reservation that an act of Congress cut into six pieces in 1889, before he was taken east, and to a people who buried some three hundred dead on Wounded Knee Creek while he was in the Minnesota cell.
suggested_refs: Fort Bennett, post and agency headquarters at the mouth of the Cheyenne River

stops.name: Cheyenne River Agency, the last documented years
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from the residence the sources imply between his return in August 1891 and the death year Hardorff gives; no dated entry covers these years
stops.campa: He lives out what is documented of his life under the Cheyenne River Agency, near Cherry Creek, among the Miniconjou and Sans Arc bands whose names the later records attach to his. He is in his middle forties. The buffalo are gone from the plains and the last free camps came in fifteen years ago. The men who fought at the Greasy Grass are being interviewed and photographed by the government whose column they destroyed, and what they say about that day is written down by the officers of it.

stops.name: Cheyenne River Agency, the death that will not stay put
stops.date_confidence: irreconcilable: Hardorff gives the year 1894 and the place Cheyenne River but no day, and elsewhere gives 1896 and 1910; the fourteenth of November comes only from an uncited Wikipedia infobox whose death_place field is empty
stops.campa: Hardorff sets his death at the Cheyenne River Agency in 1894 and does not give a day. The fourteenth of November comes from an encyclopedia field that cites nothing for it and leaves the place blank. Hardorff himself gives 1896 in one place and 1910 in another. No burial has been located: no grave, no marker, no cemetery entry in anything reachable, and the one database that might hold a listing returns an error and refuses the connection. A man photographed at least four times has no known place in the ground.

stops.name: Standing Rock, Joshua Low Dog in the 1900 census
stops.date_confidence: 1900 federal census attested; the pool presented this household as an 1890 Cherry Creek record with a daughter named Regina, and both the date and the daughter are corrected here
stops.campa: Six years after the death Hardorff records, the federal census taker at Standing Rock writes down Joshua Low Dog, age fifty-two, with his wife Louise, whose Lakota name is Tiolutawin, and three children: Louise at eighteen, Luke at fifteen, Jessie at thirteen. Either the man is alive and the death date is wrong, or a namesake is being counted, or one of the two records is an error. Nothing in the sources decides it. The household on that page is the most detailed picture of his life anywhere in the record.

stops.name: Standing Rock, the 1910 census and five tribal names
stops.date_confidence: 1910 federal census attested; the pool located this entry at Cheyenne River, which no source supports, and the coordinate is corrected to Fort Yates
stops.campa: Ten years on, the census at Standing Rock lists Joshua Low Dog again, age sixty-one, a widower, with his son Luke and his daughter Louise, and enters him as Sans Arc. He Dog, who fought in the same valley on the same day, said flatly that Low Dog was an Oglala. An interpreter called him a northern chief of the Lame Deer band. A tribal history says Siha Sapa. Another account says Minneconjou. Wikipedia says Oglala. The form says Sans Arc, and the form was filled out by a clerk.
stops.quote: Low Dog is always listed as an Oglala but is a Siha Sapa. His family went south and Cheyenne River Sioux tribal member Carideo Low Dog of Dupree, SD is the great grandson of Chief Low Dog.
stops.quote_source: Donovin A. Sprague, Standing Rock Sioux (Arcadia, 2004), p. 56, quoted on american-tribes.com

stops.name: Standing Rock, the record stops
stops.date_confidence: one account has him resident at Standing Rock through at least 1920 and stops there; this is the last year any source claims for him and no document supports or refutes it
stops.campa: He goes out of the records somewhere after 1910. One account keeps him resident at Standing Rock through at least 1920 and then stops. There is no death notice, no agency entry closing the file, no stone. The clean date in the encyclopedia and the census lines that run twenty-six years past it cannot both be counting the same life, and nothing has been produced that says which of them is counting Low Dog. The record ends the way it began, without a place and without a day.
suggested_refs: The unreconciled span between the 1894 death date and the residence claim running to 1920

stops.name: Dupree, the great-grandson on the reservation
stops.date_confidence: the statement is dated only by its source, Sprague's 2004 book; the pool's coordinate for Dupree was about 16 km off and is corrected here
stops.campa: On the Cheyenne River reservation, in Ziebach County, a tribal member named Carideo Low Dog is recorded as the great-grandson of the chief. The family went south from Standing Rock and stayed south. The line runs on in the same country that holds the ledgers, the census pages, the arrest at Cherry Creek, and the last documented years of the man himself. The paper record of that man cannot agree on the year he left it. The family can name the generations between him and a living address.

stops.name: Little Bighorn Battlefield, the field that keeps no stone for him
stops.date_confidence: the LaPointe petition is dated in sitting_bull.journey.json; the canonical battlefield pin is inherited from that file byte-identical
stops.campa: On the field the red granite markers are set only for warriors documented as killed in the fighting, so there is no stone here for a man who rode off it alive. The Indian Memorial on the ridge names the nations and not the survivors. In 2021 Sitting Bull's great-grandson Ernie LaPointe petitions to have Sitting Bull's remains brought to this ground, where the column was destroyed. A hundred and forty-five years after the afternoon, the question of who lies where on this hillside is still open, and Low Dog is not in the answer.
suggested_refs: The Indian Memorial and the red granite warrior markers, Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument
